# Replacing the flat result fields with the new format: tradeoffs

**Recommendation:** don't do a full replacement yet. Store one source of truth, and have the renderer read the flat fields through a function that computes them from it. Decide after the 46 queued jobs come back, since no committed result has the new blocks yet.

## What the code actually does today

- **The derivation runs the other way from the brief's default.** Open question 1 assumed the flat fields would be "computed from the new block". In fact `conclusion_record()` builds the conclusion from the flat fields (`verdict`, `properties`, `configurations`, `modelContracts`). Today the new blocks are a summary of the flat result.
- **The new blocks are thin.** `claim`, `attempt`, `conclusion` and `bundle` hold identities, fingerprints, statuses per obligation, and file hashes. The evidence itself has no home there: counterexamples and witnesses, TLC traces, coverage, `contractDiff`, `proof`, `statesExplored`, the before/after excerpts. So "replacing the flat fields" really means designing an evidence section per obligation, not deleting 27 keys.
- **Few things read the result.** Only `build.py`'s renderer reads it (about 40 distinct fields, `verdict` 22 times), plus its tests. The router reads it to write `index.json`, and `find.py` reads only `index.json`. `pipeline.py` reads build.py's stdout signals, not the examples' `result.json`. The blog uses session traces, not results.

## What it's about

Both reviews put the same thing first: **some Java behaviour the native engine doesn't implement is approximated instead of refused, so a false claim can come back `Verified`.** I checked this at HEAD and it still holds:
- An unresolved JDK constructor is skipped, a `void` JDK instance method does nothing, and one that returns a reference gets a fresh opaque object.
- `synchronized` does no null check.
- Fields are looked up by name alone, so a subclass field that hides a superclass one is treated as the same field.

So the brief's order is: make every `Verified` trustworthy, then make the result say exactly what was proved, then measure, and only then optimize.

## The phases

1. **Refuse what isn't implemented.**
   - A table of every instruction and call path: implemented, modelled or refused.

> &lt;/pasted_content id="d132">

> *… (shortened; the log has the full text)*

**Reply:**

Short answer: checking these properly costs very little at run time. What it costs is coverage: programs the engine accepts today would be refused. Your third option fits that well, provided the LLM proposes and the tool checks.

## What each fix costs at run time

| Gap | The proper fix | Run-time cost |
|---|---|---|
| A JDK constructor or method the engine doesn't model (skipped, a no-op, or a fresh opaque object) | Refuse it by name | **Lower.** The path stops early. |
| `synchronized` with no null check | One null check, then nothing (single-threaded) | One branch per monitor, which is rare |
| Fields looked up by name alone | Look the field up by its declaring class when the bytecode is read | Nothing during the proof |
| String and class literals as fresh objects | One object per distinct literal | Nothing to speak of |
| Static initializers never run | Refuse, or record an "already initialized" assumption | Nothing. Actually running them could be expensive, but neither option does. |
| JBMC's own stubs | Read its warnings, or one preflight run | Free, or a few seconds |
| **Having JBMC confirm a native `Verified`** | A second engine re-proves it | **Expensive.** On the recorded examples JBMC is often 10–100× slower: 141 took 2 s native against 101 s, and 142 ran JBMC out of memory. |

So "fully verify" isn't expensive because of the semantic fixes. Only the cross-engine confirmation is, and that's already optional in the draft (open question 2).
